items.originalTitle: Running Kimi K3 on MI355X at Better Performance per Dollar Than B300
items.summary:
Wafer.ai reports running the large Kimi K3 open source AI model, with 2.8 trillion parameters, on AMD MI355X GPUs, which have 288GB VRAM and cost significantly less than Nvidia B300 and B200 GPUs. Despite AMD's software challenges, Wafer.ai optimized kernel and model performance to achieve over 3.8 times the throughput per node compared to their Nvidia B200 setup and better cost efficiency than the B300.

The MI355X's high memory capacity allows it to serve the large Kimi K3 model on a single node, avoiding the cross-node overhead seen with Nvidia B200 configurations. Wafer.ai addressed initial software issues such as missing kernel functions on ROCm and improved speculative decoding and prefill performance, resulting in substantial throughput gains and competitive latency. This demonstrates AMD GPUs as a cost-effective alternative for serving frontier large language models despite initial software limitations.

items.title: PublicDomainReview explores the Ars Notoria, a medieval manuscript promising rapid mastery of knowledge through magical diagrams and prayers, despite church condemnation
items.originalTitle: Artificial Intelligence: Ars Notoria and the Promise of Instant Knowledge
items.summary:
The Ars Notoria is a medieval text that claimed to accelerate learning through complex diagrams, incantations, and rituals, offering contact with spiritual forces and divine knowledge. Although condemned by theologians like St. Thomas Aquinas as futile and demonic, the manuscript persisted in religious institutions and was copied and printed into the early modern period.

The text's unique approach involved symbolic and geometric patterns combined with prayers in ancient languages, aiming to grant scholars instant knowledge without years of study. Its survival and continued interest highlight the tension between medieval scholarly ambition and church doctrine regarding superstition and magic.

items.title: Mozilla publishes inaugural State of Open Source AI report showing open models close performance gap with proprietary AI but capture only 4% of revenue [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mozilla's Inaugural 'State of Open Source AI' Report Is Here
items.summary:
Mozilla's first State of Open Source AI report reveals that open AI models have narrowed the performance gap with leading proprietary systems like ChatGPT to 3%, while costs have dropped up to 50 times in three years. Despite powering about a third of real-world AI usage, open models capture only 4% of the revenue, highlighting a disconnect between value and financial return to the open ecosystem.

The report, based on a global survey of over 950 developers, finds that Asia leads in open source AI adoption at 89%, with governments in the EU, Canada, and India investing in open AI infrastructure as a strategic asset. While 79% of developers use open models, only 51% have deployed them in production due to missing infrastructure and tooling. Mozilla emphasizes that control over the software layer managing AI behavior is becoming more important than the models themselves, warning that without investment in governance and infrastructure, closed AI systems may dominate, limiting public interest and technological sovereignty.

items.summary:
Pluralistic explores how corporate leaders often overstate AI's transformative effects on business due to pressures to align with optimistic narratives and avoid job risks. The article draws on insights from Nikhil Suresh of Hermit Tech, who has spoken with hundreds of executives and employees revealing a pattern of AI hype that lacks concrete evidence of significant change.

Suresh highlights a coordination problem where executives feel compelled to affirm AI's benefits to preserve their positions, even when actual gains are limited. This dynamic leads to a cycle of mutual reinforcement of AI optimism despite skepticism among subordinates, contributing to what is described as "AI mania" in corporate decision-making.

items.title: EU AI Act requires labeling of AI-generated deepfakes and interactive AI systems starting August 2, with compliance deadlines extending to December
items.originalTitle: August Is Here: Time Has Come to Label AI Deepfakes
items.summary:
The European Union's AI Act mandates that AI-generated or manipulated content that could be mistaken for real, including deepfakes and interactive AI systems like chatbots, must be clearly labeled starting August 2. This transparency requirement aims to help users identify synthetic media and distinguish it from human-generated content, with a grace period until December 2 for existing generative AI tools to implement machine-readable labels.

The rules apply broadly to providers and deployers whose AI outputs are used within the EU, including those outside the region if their content targets EU audiences. Exemptions exist for artistic, satirical, fictional, or editorially reviewed AI-generated text. A Code of Practice developed by independent experts supports compliance, though enforcement and adherence by large platforms and foreign providers remain to be seen.

items.title: EU launches voluntary Code of Practice for transparency of AI-generated content starting August 2026 to support compliance with AI Act Article 50 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content (Starting August)
items.summary:
Starting August 2026, the European Union will implement a voluntary Code of Practice to enhance transparency in AI-generated content, supporting compliance with the AI Act's legal obligations on marking and labeling such content. The code, developed by independent experts and stakeholders, provides practical guidelines for providers and deployers of generative AI systems to mark AI outputs and label deepfakes, aiming to reduce administrative burdens and increase trust across EU member states.

The Code of Practice complements the AI Act's transparency requirements under Article 50, addressing risks of deception and manipulation in digital communications. While adherence to the code is voluntary, it offers a recognized framework for demonstrating compliance, with signatories collaborating through task forces to share best practices. By the end of July 2026, around 190 organizations had signed the code, which includes provisions for machine-readable marking and detection of AI-generated content and guidelines for labeling AI-manipulated text and media.

items.originalTitle: Is paying artists enough to convince them to embrace AI?
items.summary:
Pippa, a new AI startup, offers a text-to-video service that compensates artists with royalties whenever their style is used in generated content, aiming to address ethical concerns in generative AI. The company has signed agreements with a few artists and pays them per image and video second generated, alongside a share of subscription revenue, but payments remain modest compared to user fees.

Despite its ethical positioning, Pippa's technology still relies partly on models initially trained on internet-scraped art without explicit consent, reflecting a broader challenge in the AI industry. The company hopes to transition fully to artist-provided datasets but faces skepticism from artists wary of community backlash and the legacy of unauthorized training practices.

Pippa's founders compare their approach to the music industry's shift from piracy to paid streaming, aiming to set a new standard for AI content generation that respects creators' rights. However, the platform is still early-stage with limited artist participation and must overcome both technical and cultural hurdles to gain wider acceptance among artists and users.

items.originalTitle: Australian booksellers raise alarm over destruction of rare titles to feed AI
items.summary:
Australian secondhand booksellers have raised concerns that rare and valuable books are being destroyed to supply data for generative AI training. The practice, revealed in a US lawsuit against AI company Anthropic, involves buying physical books, scanning them after removing spines, and then pulping the remains, which some Australian vendors suspect is happening through intermediaries placing large, atypical orders.

Several booksellers reported receiving bulk orders from a Canadian company called Zoom Books, which buys a wide range of titles, including rare and niche items, often without regard to price. While some sellers see the sales as beneficial for clearing stock, they worry about the loss of unique cultural artifacts and the ethical implications of destroying physical books for AI data. The issue highlights tensions between copyright law, AI development, and preservation of literary heritage.

items.title: Why Apple Should Buy Granola [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Apple Should Buy Granola
items.summary:
• The Big Read: Silicon Valley looks to a new biotech frontier—Montana 

• Garry Tan’s political dreams require this 32-year-old’s ‘grunt’ force 

• Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “Dead Rabbit,” “The Amateur” and “The Drama”

Here’s a thought that would’ve seemed startling not long ago: There’s a very good chance that someone secretly recorded you this week with the help of AI. If it didn’t happen this week, it will almost certainly happen sometime in the very near future—then continue to happen with greater and greater frequency. 

And if you weren’t the one unknowingly recorded, you might have been the one pushing the record button, and you probably didn’t think twice about it. Because here’s another thought that once would have seemed extraordinary: Despite what would seem like obvious privacy invasion concerns, no one seems all too bothered by the trend—and the AI note-taking apps fueling it.

Of those apps, one of the most popular is Granola, which records a meeting, autogenerates notes from it and suggests follow-up tasks. It can be used for in-person meetings, and it also syncs seamlessly with software like Zoom and Google Meet. And really, I think it’s a pretty clear comment on the app’s caliber that anyone would rather use Granola than rely on the note-taking features Zoom and Google Meet offer. (People like it for a variety of factors, including the fact that it records digital meetings unobtrusively: No one in a Google Meet would know you’re using it—it doesn’t join the meeting as a participant or put up a recording banner.) 

Granola is especially well liked especially in Silicon Valley, where the VC crowd has proselytized it. In a testament to Granola’s quality, the company accomplished a real feat a couple of days ago: It released a version of its app for the Apple Watch, and all of a sudden, people were  talking online about the Apple Watch as an honest-to-goodness must-have gadget. 

“We’ve had a lot of emails saying, ‘I’m gonna go out and buy a Watch because of this’ or ‘Time to pull my Watch out of the drawer,’” said Granola co-founder Sam Stephenson. 

When was the last time Apple managed to release an attention-grabbing AI feature—or make the Apple Watch seem cool? Certainly not anytime in recent memory. So here’s what I think should happen: Apple should buy Granola. 

Like the best Apple products, Granola is beloved by its fans—many bands would love to have such dedicated groupies—for its sleek, well-designed simplicity. And the startup has just proven it can breathe new life into an Apple product that has seemed dull for years. Apple needs people who can pull off such a task, having chosen to heavily rely on updates to a few core products in recent years. (Granted, maybe incoming CEO John Ternus will shift that mindset a bit; meanwhile, Apple is reportedly working on smart glasses, as well as a wearable AI pin.) 

Perhaps most importantly, Granola can be probably acquired for the type of price Apple likes to pay: The company does not do mega-acquisitions. Granola, founded in 2023, most recently got a $1.5 billion valuation in a March fundraising, which included Index Ventures, Kleiner Perkins and other investors. 

Granola’s attention-catching Apple Watch debut was something of a happy accident, Stephenson said. The app was originally a side project of Tom Humphrey, a Granola software engineer, that gained momentum within the company after he bolstered enthusiasm for it with a surprising revelation: The data Granola accessed about its iOS users showed that 40% of them also owned an Apple Watch. 

Among Granola staff, the Apple Watch app has quickly become much more popular than the iPhone one. “You just think to turn it on much more often than you do with the iPhone,” Stephenson said. “The worst thing about the iPhone app is that it’s in your pocket: out of sight, out of mind. You forget to use it.”

Granola has toyed with the thought of making its own hardware but has shied away from doing so. Whatever the startup released would face stiff competition from the growing number of already available devices dedicated to AI note-taking. Plaud, a five-year-old startup, makes one of the most popular ones. 

I first wrote about Granola and AI note-taking last year when it seemed like the dawn of a new always-on, always-recording world. It’s now something like sunshiny midmorning: Over the past year, Granola’s user growth has been a “smooth curve: upward and to the right,” said Stephenson. (He declined to give specifics.) Meanwhile, the startup has gone from two floors of a Shoreditch, London, office to occupying the entire building, roughly quintupling its staff to nearly 100.

Given Granola’s rising popularity, I asked Stephenson if he had met any unexpected users. “Well, Gwyneth Paltrow comes to mind,” he said.—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

The Big Read

Silicon Valley Looks to a New Biotech Frontier: Montana

The state is now allowing anyone—not just the very sick—to access unapproved, experimental drugs. It’s a boon for biotech startups and an overt embrace of the tech world ethos for cutting back on rules that might limit innovation.

Forrest Liu is tasked with an agenda that focuses on local Bay Area candidates, economic growth—and the death of the billionaire’s tax.

Listening: “Dead Rabbit” 

As a genre of fiction, folk horror has given us memorable entertainment such as “Midsommar” and “The Wicker Man.” “Dead Rabbit,” a podcast from BBC Radio 4, is the rare nonfiction version: Hosts Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor, a husband-and-wife pair of investigative journalists, set off into the countryside to figure out why piles of mangled animals keep getting threateningly piled up around Awbridge, England, a well-heeled, 757-person community. It’s a place full of well-tended flower baskets and a chipper vicar, who tries to turn the first grisly mise-en-scène he encounters on his parish doorstep—a severed deer’s head—into a joke about venison sausages. Not everyone in the clergyman’s flock is as determinedly upbeat, and the carcasses have thoroughly disturbed much of the village, sparking WhatsApp groups replete with theories (devil worship, perhaps?) and recriminations. The series begins as a spotlight on what happens within the unnerved small town and then widens its focus to larger issues of conservation, animal cruelty and liberal-versus-conservative politics. Squished roadkill has never seemed more sinister.—Abram Brown

Reading: “The Amateur” by Chris Bohjalian 

After three decades and 24 novels, Chris Bohjalian has established himself as an ultrareliable source of highbrow potboilers. More often than not, he likes to get them going with a real bang. Or, as he described it in a 2018 conversation with The New York Times, he likes an opening moment of “cataclysmic disequilibrium.”

Just such a catastrophe unfolds in the first few pages of “The Amateur,” his latest and probably finest novel. On Aug. 3, 1978, Mira Wilston, a privileged teenage golf prodigy from a tony Westchester, N.Y., suburb, sends a well-struck drive straight through a practice net—and it zings right into the head of a nearby caddie: Kenny, a high school classmate. It kills him instantly. So who deserves the blame? Mira, who narrates the tale? The country club? The net’s manufacturer? Had Bohjalian been thinking less ambitiously, he would’ve kept his exploration of culpability and responsibility confined to the immediate damage from Mira’s errant shot (in a tale embellished by nice period-piece details, like the high school’s smoking lounge and the Miami Sound Machine records). But he wasn’t and he didn’t. In the accident’s aftermath, the disequilibrium intensifies—as Kenny’s demise inadvertently leads to the public revelation of a long-running sexual relationship between Mira, 18, and one of the country club dads. Yes, it should sound a little like “Lolita,” and therein lies the greater conceit of “The Amateur,” which appropriates and restyles Vladimir Nabokov’s classic, widening to an examination of power, control and fate. The connection between the two novels is an explicit one: Mira, who recounts all the events with a meta, tragicomic awareness, remarks on it several times.—A.B.

Watching: “The Drama”

An admission I make with no degree of hyperbole: I watched several parts of “The Drama,” an A24 film starring Robert Pattinson and Zendaya as a pair of engaged lovebirds, with my mouth fully agape. And when the tension between them ratcheted up further, I watched through gaps between my fingers: I’d thrown a hand over my eyes. What can I say? Scenes of matrimonial Armageddon make me squirm, and “The Drama” (newly streaming on HBO Max) goes full-on scorched earth. 

To explain the plot in much detail would ruin the film, so to summarize it quickly: Shortly before their big day, a secret-telling drinking game goes horribly awry when Emma (Zendaya) reveals a dark moment from her past that shocks Charlie (Pattinson). I don’t blame him—it shocked me, too, and what’s more surprising is that the film does the reveal quite quickly. (Drew Barrymore survived only marginally longer in “Scream.”) Mostly, “The Drama” devotes itself to chronicling the subsequent fallout—with director Kristoffer Borgli twisting the usual rhythms of a screwball rom-com into devious knots.

As an unmarried 37-year-old who has needed to soldier through more than a dozen friend weddings in the last decade, I also appreciated how “The Drama” very neatly satirizes how millennials have turned the exchanging of vows into an industrial nuptial complex.—A.B.

After three decades and 24 novels, Chris Bohjalian has established himself as an ultrareliable source of highbrow potboilers. More often than not, he likes to get them going with a real bang. Or, as he described it in a 2018 conversation with The New York Times, he likes an opening moment of “cataclysmic disequilibrium.”

Just such a catastrophe unfolds in the first few pages of “The Amateur,” his latest and probably finest novel. On Aug. 3, 1978, Mira Wilston, a privileged teenage golf prodigy from a tony Westchester, N.Y., suburb, sends a well-struck drive straight through a practice net—and it zings right into the head of a nearby caddie: Kenny, a high school classmate. It kills him instantly. So who deserves the blame? Mira, who narrates the tale? The country club? The net’s manufacturer? Had Bohjalian been thinking less ambitiously, he would’ve kept his exploration of culpability and responsibility confined to the immediate damage from Mira’s errant shot (in a tale embellished by nice period-piece details, like the high school’s smoking lounge and the Miami Sound Machine records). But he wasn’t and he didn’t. In the accident’s aftermath, the disequilibrium intensifies—as Kenny’s demise inadvertently leads to the public revelation of a long-running sexual relationship between Mira, 18, and one of the country club dads. Yes, it should sound a little like “Lolita,” and therein lies the greater conceit of “The Amateur,” which appropriates and restyles Vladimir Nabokov’s classic, widening to an examination of power, control and fate. The connection between the two novels is an explicit one: Mira, who recounts all the events with a meta, tragicomic awareness, remarks on it several times.—A.B.

An admission I make with no degree of hyperbole: I watched several parts of “The Drama,” an A24 film starring Robert Pattinson and Zendaya as a pair of engaged lovebirds, with my mouth fully agape. And when the tension between them ratcheted up further, I watched through gaps between my fingers: I’d thrown a hand over my eyes. What can I say? Scenes of matrimonial Armageddon make me squirm, and “The Drama” (newly streaming on HBO Max) goes full-on scorched earth. 

To explain the plot in much detail would ruin the film, so to summarize it quickly: Shortly before their big day, a secret-telling drinking game goes horribly awry when Emma (Zendaya) reveals a dark moment from her past that shocks Charlie (Pattinson). I don’t blame him—it shocked me, too, and what’s more surprising is that the film does the reveal quite quickly. (Drew Barrymore survived only marginally longer in “Scream.”) Mostly, “The Drama” devotes itself to chronicling the subsequent fallout—with director Kristoffer Borgli twisting the usual rhythms of a screwball rom-com into devious knots.

As an unmarried 37-year-old who has needed to soldier through more than a dozen friend weddings in the last decade, I also appreciated how “The Drama” very neatly satirizes how millennials have turned the exchanging of vows into an industrial nuptial complex.—A.B.
